Thank you for revising and resubmitting your article "Social groups buffer maternal loss in mountain gorillas" for consideration by eLife. Your article and response have been evaluated by a Guest Editor and Christian Rutz as the Senior Editor.

We would like to draw your attention to changes in our revision policy that we have made in response to COVID-19 (https://elifesciences.org/articles/57162). Specifically, we are asking Editors to quickly process manuscripts, like yours, that they judge can potentially stand as eLife papers without additional data. Thus, the revisions requested below are aimed at (a) addressing clarity and presentation of the manuscript, and (b) addressing further considerations about the current analyses and arising conclusions.

As outlined in the first decision letter, this manuscript provides an "in-depth assessment of the consequences of maternal loss for wild mountain gorillas" and was found to be a "rigorous and detailed examination" that was appreciated by the Editors and all the reviewers. During the first assessment by the reviewers and Editors, some potential problems with the wording of particular parts of the text were raised, and this revision appears to address all of these in full. However, the first assessment also raised some issues with the reported analyses, and unfortunately, there is still some lack-of-clarity and some issues that need to be resolved. To outline these issues in as clear a way as possible, the below text takes a 3-step approach for each issue: (A) it revisits the initial comment, (B) provides the authors' response (and associated manuscript text), and finally (C) describes why a problem still exists and what needs to be addressed.

1) Differences in social changes

1A) Revisiting the issue: "The use of paired t-tests for the examination of social changes is a bit confusing here. Specifically -on my part- I'm unsure how these properly control for repeated sampling of individuals when considering changes in dyadic association scores? Also, the changes reported here appear to just assess how orphan behaviour altered between the pre- and the post- maternal loss period, but how do we know that such changes aren't expected anyway over time? Ideally this analysis would directly compared orphaned to non-orphaned individuals. Note the comments from reviewer 1 about these paired t-tests need to be addressed too"

1B) Author response: "Yes, we entirely agree and have changed these analyses to instead compare whether network metrics (binary degree, weighted degree and eigenvector centrality) change differently in orphans relative to other immature gorillas within the same group during the same time period using node-based permutations constrained to swap only between individuals within the same incident of maternal loss (based on the same pair of networks). Described in the Materials and methods and Results."

1C) Current Issue:

While we appreciate that the authors have taken the first comment onboard and reconsidered the approach, there are two remaining problems with the current approach. Namely:

1Ci) In the Results, the results of these tests are reported. But, when reporting these results, it is important to not entirely focus on the p-value generated from the null models, but to also report the full results of the standard statistical test as well (i.e., the estimate, the SE, the t value, and the standard p-value). The p-value from the null model is simply used to 'double-check' the results of the standard statistical test, and shouldn't be fully relied upon for conclusions like this. For example, the first result reported here is "(t=1.721,p=0.029)" which isn't clear to the reader, as a t-value this low wouldn't generally result in a p-value this low. Instead, the text needs to report the actual observed statistical test results from the standard test (including the real p-value) and then also include a Pnull value (the null value generated from the node permutations). If the primary standard statistical test shows no significant difference (as may be the case here), then this primary result should be relied upon for drawing conclusions (not the null model p-value, as this is mainly just for double-checking tests, rather than drawing direct conclusions from them in this particular way).

Also, as a small side-point, the method used here for actually calculating the node permutation p-value is quite a strange one. Specifically, it is stated in the revised text that "two-tailed p-values were calculated as two times the proportion of permutation t-values greater or smaller than the t-value from the real data set". But this is problematic and doesn't make clear sense? What is actually being done here?

1Cii) The text goes on to state that "within contact-based networks orphans did not show these same gains, with no significant increase in binary degree (t=0.099, p=0.730), weighted degree (t=1.110, p=0.397) or eigenvector centrality (t=0.129, p=0.741) relative to non-orphans". But it isn't clear where these results are actually derived from. We are assuming that they come from a subset of tests the authors refer to in their response, i.e., 'node-based permutations constrained to swap only between individuals within the same incident of maternal loss'. But, if the swaps are constrained between individuals who experience the same incident of maternal loss, and you subsequently try to look at the comparable difference between incident of maternal loss, then the tests will never find a difference because this is already controlled for earlier in the pipeline? Some clarity about what is actually going on here needs to be added to the manuscript (and also some thought about whether such tests are appropriate for testing the questions at hand).

2) Social networks and observations

2A) Revisiting the issue: The first assessment of the paper flagged up that animal social networks are strongly influenced by observation, and requested some analytical consideration of this in the revisions.

2B) Author Response: The authors responded by providing more details about the data collection methods, which is very much appreciated. However, the revision doesn't include any attempts to actually control for/integrate consideration of differences in observation number. Instead, the response states that the Simple Ratio Index includes this (stating "variation in the number of focal scans per individual which is accounted for within the simple ratio index" and "we did not believe that these extra data would bias the estimate of the specific relationships based on SRI (as these account for the total number of observations)".

2C) Current Issue: Unfortunately, the SRI does not control for differences in observation number in the way that the authors lay out here. While the SRI takes some of the difference in observation into account during the calculation of the dyadic values, it in no way fully accounts for this; it just uses it for the calculation. For instance, even in simulations where all individuals have the same social phenotype, those individuals which are observed more will have higher centrality (e.g., higher degree) than those which are observed less. This is simply a product of how these metrics are calculated and how these networks emerge. Therefore, the previous comments from the Editors and the reviewers that the analyses should directly consider 'observation number' still stands.

3) Outstanding analytical issues

3A/B) Revisiting the issue: In the reviewer comments, a few analytical (smaller) issues were pointed out, and in most cases the authors have addressed these fully and clearly. However, a couple of key points remain. Particularly, controlling for age and network differences within the models themselves, and also using 'change in metric' as the response.

3C) Current Issue: The revision didn't make any attempt to actually integrate age of individuals into the models, nor did it try to consider network groups, but the reviewers made solid points that these would be good to consider. We believe these should be integrated into the paper as supplementary analyses. Finally, the switch to considering “change in metric” as the response is certainly useful in lots of ways, but have the authors' considered problems with “regression to the mean” in this sense? Specifically, we can automatically expect this metric to be altered significantly by the initial value, whereby those which initially have a large SN metric value are likely to (just by chance) have large -ve change values, and whereby those which initially have a small SN metric value are likely to (just by chance) have large +ve change values. Have the authors assessed this as a driver/contributor to the results here? (Note this consideration relates to the above point about considering things like age, and network group, which might alter these initial values and thus affect the change values.)

results.result: Maternal loss after age 2 does not significantly reduce survival in mountain gorillas. Cox-proportional hazards analysis and Bayesian survival trajectory analysis found no significant differences in survival between orphan classes (infants, juveniles, subadults) and non-orphans for both sexes, with the null model showing highest support.
results.evaluation: Claims C92 and C93 provide direct statistical evidence from two independent analytical approaches (Cox-proportional hazards and Bayesian survival trajectory analysis) showing no significant survival differences. While C154 acknowledges sample size limitations (n=59 orphans), C155 notes that comparable sample sizes detected effects in other species, strengthening the interpretation that effects are genuinely absent or very weak (C156). The convergence of multiple statistical approaches supports this conclusion.

results.result: Maternal loss has no significant effect on age at first birth in female mountain gorillas. Orphaned females gave birth slightly younger (9.67-9.72 years) than non-orphans (10.24 years), a pattern consistent with the stress acceleration hypothesis, though the effect was not statistically significant.
results.evaluation: Claim C101 provides direct statistical evidence of no significant effect using generalized linear models. The descriptive statistics (C102-C104) show the direction of effect, and C161 notes the non-significant trend. Claims C163-C164 appropriately contextualize this as consistent with stress acceleration theory while acknowledging lack of statistical significance. The result is well-supported by appropriate statistical testing.

results.result: Maternal loss does not significantly affect survival of first offspring through infancy in female mountain gorillas. First offspring of orphaned females showed marginally higher survival (57-60%) compared to non-orphans (51.5%), but this difference was not statistically significant after controlling for age at first birth and dispersal.
results.evaluation: Claim C105 provides direct statistical evidence using binomial generalized linear models with appropriate controls. The descriptive statistics (C106-C108) show the actual survival rates, and C162 notes the non-significant trend. The statistical approach appropriately accounts for potential confounders (age at first birth, dispersal), strengthening the conclusion.

results.result: Maternal loss affects dispersal decisions differently by age and sex. Females orphaned as juveniles/subadults showed a near-significant increase in dispersal likelihood (75% vs 37.5% for non-orphans, p=0.072). Males orphaned as juveniles/subadults were significantly more likely to disperse before age 16 (84.6% vs 37.5%, p=0.008).
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C95 report appropriate statistical testing for females with borderline significance. Claim C100 provides strong statistical evidence for males (p=0.008). The descriptive statistics (C96-C98) support the patterns. However, the female result is marginally below conventional significance thresholds, which is appropriately noted. The sex difference in statistical significance is clearly documented.

results.result: Maternal loss shows age-dependent effects on male dominance attainment. All three infant-orphaned males became dominant by age 23, while no juvenile/subadult-orphaned males (n=5) achieved dominance by this age, compared to 52% of non-orphans. However, 71% of younger juvenile/subadult-orphaned males (age 16-23) had already become dominant, indicating capacity for later dominance attainment.
results.evaluation: The descriptive statistics (C109-C115) show clear patterns, but the authors explicitly acknowledge that small sample sizes prevented statistical testing (C171). While the pattern mirrors dispersal effects (C172), and C169-C170 demonstrate that orphans can achieve dominance, the lack of statistical testing and very small sample sizes (especially n=3 infant orphans, n=5 juvenile/subadult orphans) make it impossible to determine if observed differences are statistically meaningful or due to chance.

results.result: Following maternal loss, orphans' proximity-based social relationships strengthen significantly. Orphans showed significantly greater increases in eigenvector centrality (p<0.001) and weighted degree (p=0.021) compared to non-orphans, resulting in similar network positions post-loss despite losing a key social partner.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C125 provide strong statistical evidence using GAMMs with node-level permutations, an appropriate method for network data. Both parametric (p<0.001, p=0.021) and permutation-based (Pnull<0.001, Pnull=0.024) tests support the findings. Claim C126 demonstrates the biological significance: orphans achieve similar network positions to non-orphans post-loss. The convergence of multiple network metrics strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Orphans did not show significant increases in contact-based network metrics relative to non-orphans. Neither eigenvector centrality (p=0.554) nor weighted degree (p=0.513) changed significantly more for orphans, resulting in a net 31% decrease in affiliative contact following maternal loss.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C128 provide clear statistical evidence of non-significant effects using appropriate methods (GAMMs with permutation tests). The p-values are well above conventional thresholds. Claims C122 and C195 quantify the net effect, showing that increased contact with other group members did not compensate for loss of maternal contact. This contrasts with proximity-based measures, providing important nuance.

results.result: Relationships with dominant males strengthen most following maternal loss. Both affiliative contact and proximity with dominant males increased significantly more for orphans than non-orphans, with the increase significantly greater than all other age-sex classes for contact, and greater than subordinate males for proximity.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C137 provide detailed statistical evidence from GAMMs showing which relationships strengthen (Figure 3, Supplementary Table 6). Claims C146-C148 demonstrate that dominant males show the greatest increase, with appropriate statistical comparisons across age-sex classes. The pattern is consistent across both measures of affiliation, though with some differences in statistical significance for specific comparisons. The evidence strongly supports dominant males as primary sources of social support.

results.result: Age-mates (within 2 years age difference) show greater increases in proximity with orphans after maternal loss (p=0.004), but not in affiliative contact (non-significant). The increase in proximity is smaller for older orphans (p=0.042), but age effects on contact are non-significant.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C143 provide clear statistical evidence from GAMMs (Table 5) showing differential effects by relationship type. Claims C140-C141 document age-dependent effects with appropriate statistical testing. The distinction between proximity and contact measures is important and well-documented. The statistical evidence is appropriately qualified, noting which effects are significant and which are not.

results.result: Subordinate adult males and subadult females increase affiliative contact with younger siblings following maternal loss, while siblings in other age-sex classes do not. This pattern is similar to that observed in chimpanzees.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C145 provide statistical evidence from GAMMs showing significant interaction effects (Table 5). Claim C214 appropriately contextualizes this within comparative literature (citing Reddy and Mitani 2019 on chimpanzees). The specificity of the effect to certain age-sex classes is well-documented. However, the biological mechanisms (C215, C218-C220) remain speculative.

results.result: Paternity does not influence social support from adult males after maternal loss (contact: p=0.262; proximity: p=0.583), but maternal siblings increase both contact (p<0.001) and proximity (p=0.028) more than non-siblings. This effect is driven primarily by subordinate males, while dominant males show similar support regardless of kinship.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C151 provide clear statistical evidence on paternity and sibling effects from GAMMs. Claims C152-C153 appropriately decompose the sibling effect by male dominance status (Supplementary Table 7, Figure 3—supplement 2). Claim C212 contextualizes this within prior findings on paternal care. The statistical evidence is strong, though the sample size for paternity analysis is limited (n=18 orphans with known paternity, C149).

results.result: Binary degree (number of social connections) did not increase more for orphans than non-orphans in either contact or proximity networks, suggesting orphans strengthen existing bonds rather than forming new ones.
results.evaluation: Claim C129 provides statistical evidence from GAMMs (Supplementary Table 5). Claim C191 appropriately interprets this as strengthening existing relationships rather than forming new ones. This interpretation is logical given the increases in weighted degree without increases in binary degree. The distinction between relationship strength and number is important for understanding the social response mechanism.

results.result: The extent to which orphans' relationships with other group members strengthened following maternal loss did not differ by orphan sex for either affiliative contact or proximity.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C139 report non-significant sex effects from GAMMs (Table 5). This is important for demonstrating that social buffering occurs similarly for both sexes, despite sex differences in other outcomes (e.g., dispersal). The statistical testing is appropriate and the null result is clearly reported.

results.result: In mountain gorillas, maternal loss may be buffered by relationships within cohesive social groups, breaking the link between maternal loss, social adversity, and decreased fitness. This pattern resembles certain human populations and possibly killer whales, contrasting with most other social mammals where maternal loss causes considerable social adversity.
results.evaluation: This synthesis result integrates findings across multiple fitness measures (survival, reproduction) and social network analyses. Claims C177-C180 summarize fitness effects, C188 and C239 note the absence of social adversity, and C240 identifies the buffering mechanism. Claims C237 and C243 appropriately contextualize within comparative literature. However, C178 and C238 acknowledge important limitations: longer-term reproductive effects cannot be ruled out, and direct causal links between social buffering and fitness outcomes are not established. The result is well-supported but appropriately qualified.

results.result: Study limitations include: sample size (n=59 orphans) may limit detection of weak survival effects, though comparable studies found significant effects; social network analysis covers only 6 months post-loss; and direct causal links between social buffering and fitness cannot be demonstrated.
results.evaluation: These claims appropriately acknowledge study limitations. C154-C156 address statistical power concerns while contextualizing with comparative data. C226 notes the temporal limitation of social network analysis, though C227-C228 provide some evidence for longer-term persistence. C238 appropriately acknowledges the limitation in establishing causality between social changes and fitness outcomes. These are honest assessments of what the data can and cannot demonstrate.
